stories.headline: Nicki Minaj pledges to support Donald Trump again during Michigan Republican campaign rally
stories.note: A major celebrity backing Trump on stage in Michigan is a boost for the GOP in a key battleground.
body: Rapper Nicki Minaj joined President Trump onstage Sunday at a Republican rally in Port Huron, Michigan, where Trump was campaigning for Senate candidate Mike Rogers and governor candidate John James.

Minaj told the crowd she would back Trump "forever and ever" and would support him again if he ran, though the 22nd Amendment bars him from winning a third term. She credited him with changing the country's energy and giving families a brighter future to look forward to.
She also pushed voters to elect the GOP slate in Michigan, calling the midterms a major turning point, and said children should be left out of debates over gender transitions.

Trump introduced her as the "queen of rap" and joked that she was overshadowing him. White House communications director Steven Cheung later joked on X that Minaj might be the next press secretary. The appearance follows her recent Fox News interview with Lara Trump urging young Americans to vote red.
Why it matters: A major pop-culture star making the GOP case in a must-win battleground could help Republicans reach younger and less political voters in the final stretch before Election Day.

stories.headline: Dem Senate hopeful rejects Schumer but benefits from millions in spending by his allies
stories.note: A Democrat distancing from Schumer while cashing in on his allies' money hands Republicans an easy hypocrisy attack.
body: In Kansas, Democratic Senate candidate Adam Hamilton has built his campaign around saying he won't back Chuck Schumer as party leader, but national Democrats, including the Schumer-aligned Senate Majority PAC, are pouring money into the race on his behalf.

According to AdImpact figures cited by Fox, Democrats and Hamilton's campaign are on track to spend about $38 million, compared with roughly $32 million from Republicans and Sen. Roger Marshall. The Schumer-linked super PAC alone reserved $5 million in ads this month. Hamilton has also outraised Marshall, about $14 million to $6 million.
Marshall asked how Hamilton could take "$30 to $40 million from Chuck Schumer and not be beholden to him," warning that losing the seat could hand Senate control, and the leader's post, to Schumer.

Hamilton's campaign said he wants fresh leadership and will put Kansas first, and accused Marshall of relying on Washington money. Under federal law, candidates can't directly coordinate with or accept money from independent super PACs.

Why it matters: The race in ruby-red Kansas is tighter than Republicans expected, and Marshall's argument that a vote for Hamilton is a vote for a Schumer majority is the GOP's clearest path to holding the seat.

stories.headline: Bruce Blakeman calls Kathy Hochul Zohran Mamdani's 'puppet' during New York campaign rally
stories.note: Blakeman is tying Hochul to Mamdani's socialist agenda in the final stretch of the governor's race.
body: At a Sunday rally in Yorktown Heights, Republican governor candidate Bruce Blakeman, the Nassau County executive, called Gov. Kathy Hochul a "puppet" of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

Blakeman pointed to Hochul campaigning with Mamdani this week, including at a Brooklyn rally, and told her to keep bringing the democratic socialist mayor along so voters are reminded who is running the Democratic Party. He also faulted both on illegal immigration and crime.

The alliance comes as democratic socialists have gained ground in New York, with Mamdani-aligned candidates knocking off two Democratic incumbents in congressional primaries this year. Earlier this month Blakeman called Hochul the "most pro-criminal governor" during a campaign ride on the subway.
Mamdani has accused Blakeman of bigotry and racism, and Hochul and Mamdani say their focus on affordability and child care is about lowering costs for working families.
Why it matters: Tying Hochul to Mamdani's socialist agenda is Blakeman's central pitch to moderate and suburban voters who could decide whether a Republican can win statewide in New York.

stories.headline: Hochul faces revolt from unlikely New Yorkers as Democrats deliver scathing verdict on their party
stories.note: Even Democratic voters are souring on their own party, a bad sign for Hochul.
body: Bruce Blakeman is courting frustrated Democrats in his bid to unseat Gov. Kathy Hochul, and at a stop at the Crosstown Diner in the Bronx, several of them said they're on board.

Former Democratic Bronx Assemblyman Stephen Kaufman, rallying with Blakeman, said today's party leaders are "not Democrats. They're socialists and communists," and accused Hochul of moving ever further left. Bronx voters echoed complaints about rising costs, public safety and the party's direction, with one registered Democrat saying he votes for whoever helps the middle class.

Blakeman said lifelong Democrats keep telling him they've never voted Republican but will this time. He hit Hochul over tax hikes, dozens of utility rate increases and cashless bail, and pledged to cut taxes and utility bills, citing his record of not raising taxes in five years as Nassau County executive.
The article notes democratic socialists have moved into real power, from Mamdani's mayoral win to DSA-backed primary victories over Democratic incumbents in New York and Colorado.
Why it matters: If working-class Democrats in places like the Bronx break for Blakeman, Hochul's path to reelection gets a lot harder.

stories.headline: Trump immigration win could strengthen admin's hand in looming Supreme Court fight
stories.note: A court win on immigration gives Trump momentum heading into a bigger Supreme Court battle.
body: The full Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled Friday that illegal immigrants who were never formally admitted to the U.S. have no constitutional right to a bond hearing while they await deportation, a major win for the Trump administration.

The case involved three men held under the federal mandatory-detention law. The court said years or decades of living here, and ties to their communities, don't create a due process right to a bond hearing.

The ruling lands as the Supreme Court prepares to hear Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, which will settle a 9-2 split among appeals courts over whether mandatory detention applies to longtime immigrants arrested inside the country. A loss for the government there could make Friday's ruling far less significant, as dissenting Judge Leslie Southwick noted.

Conservative legal experts think the decision could help the administration. Florida State law professor Michael Morley said courts weigh whether a reading of the law would be unconstitutional, and Hans von Spakovsky said he'd be surprised if a Supreme Court majority disagreed with the Fifth Circuit.
Why it matters: The ruling strengthens Trump's hand on immigration enforcement heading into a high-stakes Supreme Court showdown.

stories.headline: Trump's fingerprints seen on Latin America's rightward shift as Brazil becomes next test
stories.note: Trump's influence is credited with a conservative wave across Latin America.
body: Fox News Digital reports that several Latin American countries have moved toward right-leaning leadership during the Trump era, and supporters credit the president, with Brazil's upcoming vote as the next big test.

Argentina-born rally-goer Marcelo Sandrin, speaking near Clemson, said Trump deserves "a lot of credit" and pointed to Argentine President Javier Milei as a leading example. Manhattan Institute researcher Santiago Vidal Calvo said the U.S. capture of Venezuela's Nicolás Maduro showed the region that America is again an influential force and that China is losing ground.
Calvo also credited Milei and El Salvador's Nayib Bukele with inspiring right-leaning movements, and praised Secretary of State Marco Rubio's Latin America strategy as an underappreciated success.
The trend isn't uniform: Mexico's left-wing Morena movement and Uruguay remain on the left, and Brazil's political future is still contested as Jair Bolsonaro's allies try to return to power.
Why it matters: A friendlier, more conservative hemisphere could help Trump on immigration, trade, drugs and pushing back on China.
